item.text: {"text":"Adaptive intent segmentation has a close recent match: [S2-CAR (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.25415) models intent as a continuous latent energy state and uses a context-aware soft temporal point process to identify boundaries through energy decay, avoiding fixed time-gap rules. It then aggregates coherent segments into multiple interest representations; the authors report that segmentation also improves existing recommendation backbones. [ScaleRec (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ipm.2025.104318) offers a complementary approach: multi-scale Transformers, dual attention for transient versus stable interests, and adaptive masking to reduce redundant interactions. [MIMAR-SRec (2026)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/38489) combines contextual windows with intent prototypes and contrastive learning, supporting multiple intent horizons rather than a single recent-interest representation. These papers motivate adaptive context selection, but do not establish gains on the pinned RecHarness evaluation.\n\nA directly relevant gating precedent, although older, is [TLSRec (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.04760): hierarchical local/global attention plus an aspect-level neural gate conditioned on elapsed time since the last interaction. Practical inference for this task: preserve SASRec’s long-term representation, add a compact intent state whose retention gate uses adjacent-item similarity and observed log time gaps, and learn a fusion gate between current-segment and historical preferences. Compare against fixed-window and learned-decay baselines; diagnose whether gains concentrate after long gaps or abrupt semantic shifts. At prediction, use only timestamps already observable in the history; do not condition on the withheld next interaction’s timestamp. Segmentation and gating can use item histories and timestamps without unavailable ratings, reviews, or simulator traits."}
